20 Things Our 90s Moms Did That We’d Never Get Away With Today

by Carly the Mommy
2 shares
  • Share
  • Tweet
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:10
Instaread

The other day, I caught myself about to yell “Be home when the streetlights come on!” to my kids. Then I remembered we live in a different world, and I’d probably get a visit from a concerned neighbor.

Our moms in the 90s parented differently. There were no parenting blogs (ha), no Facebook groups to ask, and no one filming them in the grocery store. They trusted their gut, they said “because I said so,” and they let us figure a lot of things out on our own.

Some of what they did, we’ve rightly left behind. Some of it, honestly, we could use a little more of.

MY LATEST VIDEOS

Video Paused

Here are 20 things our 90s moms did that we’d never get away with today. Read it, laugh, and then go call your mom.

1. “Be Home When the Streetlights Come On”

 

That was the only rule. We left after breakfast, rode bikes all over the neighborhood, came home for lunch, and disappeared again. Mom had no idea where we were, and she wasn’t worried.

No trackers. No texts. Just a sunset deadline.

2. Hollering Out the Back Door for Dinner

 

No phone call, no group text. Mom stepped out on the porch and yelled your name loud enough for the whole street to hear. Sometimes she rang a bell.

If you heard your middle name, you ran.

3. Letting Us Ride in the Back of the Pickup

 

A summer evening, a pile of cousins, and the wind in our hair on the way to get ice cream. It felt like the best ride at the fair.

We know so much more about car safety now, and we’re thankful for it. But we can admit it was fun.

4. The Front Seat at Age Eight

 

Calling “shotgun” was a real competition, and the winner rode up front no matter how old they were. Booster seats were for little kids, and “little” ended pretty early.

Today’s car seat rules exist for good reason. Our moms just didn’t have the research we have.

5. “I’ll Be Right Back” in the Car

 

Mom ran into the store or the bank and left us in the car with the windows cracked. We fought over the radio and messed with every button we could reach.

This is definitely one we’ve left in the 90s, and that’s a good thing.

6. Sending Us to the Corner Store Alone

 

A few dollars in our pocket and a list from Mom: milk, bread, and maybe a candy bar if we were good. We walked or biked there by ourselves at eight or nine years old.

We felt so grown up. Some of us came back with more candy than milk.

7. The House Key on a String

 

Plenty of 90s kids came home from school to an empty house, wearing a house key on a shoelace around their neck. We made our own snacks, started our homework (sort of), and watched TV until Mom got home.

We learned a lot of independence early.

8. Counting to Three

 

“One… two…” and we moved. Nobody ever found out what happened at three, and nobody wanted to.

It still works, by the way. I’ve tested it.

9. “Because I Said So”

 

No long explanations, no negotiating, no gentle parenting scripts. Just four words that ended every argument.

I try hard to explain things to my kids. But I’ll admit, I’ve used this one more than once.

10. Letting Us Lick the Beaters

 

Cookie dough, cake batter, brownie mix. Raw eggs and all, we licked every last bit off the beaters and the spoon, and sometimes the bowl.

Today it comes with a warning label. Back then, it was our reward for helping.

11. Sunscreen Once a Summer (Maybe)

 

A quick swipe of sunscreen in June, and that was it until Labor Day. Some of the teenage girls were lying out with baby oil.

We know so much more now. Reapply, friends!

12. Bike Helmets Were Optional

 

We raced down hills, jumped curbs, and rode with no hands, all with our hair blowing in the wind. Helmets existed, but nobody we knew wore one.

My kids wear theirs every time. Some changes are definitely for the better.

13. The Trampoline With No Net

 

Five kids jumping at once, double bounces, and somebody always flying off the side. The net hadn’t been invented yet, or at least nobody’s mom had bought one.

Somehow most of us survived with just a few bruises.

14. Scalding Metal Slides

 

Playgrounds were made of metal and wood, and in July, that slide could burn the backs of your legs. Add the merry-go-round that spun way too fast, and the playground was an adventure.

Today’s playgrounds are softer and safer. But we sure had fun.

15. Putting Babies to Sleep on Their Tummies

 

Back then, a lot of moms were told to put babies down on their tummies. Then in 1994, the national Back to Sleep campaign taught parents to put babies on their backs instead.

This is one of the best examples of how parenting advice changes as we learn more.

16. Peanut Butter Everywhere

 

PB&J was the official lunch of the 90s, and nobody thought twice about sending it to school. Peanut butter crackers were the go-to snack.

Now so many classrooms are nut-free, and for good reason.

17. Cartoons All Saturday Morning, No Guilt

Nobody was counting our screen time. We watched cartoons until noon, and Mom enjoyed her coffee in peace.

We worry a lot more about screens today. Our moms just called it Saturday.

18. Birthday Parties at Home With a Sheet Cake

 

A store-bought sheet cake, a few balloons, and pin the tail on the donkey in the backyard. No theme, no balloon arch, no matching plates.

And it was the best birthday party ever. (Says the woman who writes about baby shower themes. I see the irony.)

19. The Licked-Thumb Face Wipe

 

You had a speck of something on your cheek, and before you could run, Mom licked her thumb and scrubbed it off. In public. In front of everyone.

I swore I’d never do it. I have done it.

20. Sitting on the Bleachers, Not Filming Everything

 

Our moms watched our games and recitals with their own eyes, not through a screen. Most of those moments only live in our memories now.

Honestly? This might be the one I want to bring back the most.

Thank You, 90s Moms

Our moms weren’t perfect, and they’d be the first to say so. They didn’t have the research, the resources, or the endless advice we have today. But they loved us fiercely, they gave us freedom, and they trusted us to figure things out.

I’m keeping the car seats and the bike helmets. But I’m also trying to keep a little of that 90s mom confidence, the kind that didn’t need anyone’s approval to know she was doing a good job.

Which of these did your mom do? And which one are you secretly still doing? Tell me in the comments. No judgment here!
